Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: Fact-checking plays a vital role in information validation, serving as a crucial defence against the widespread dissemination of misinformation and disinformation. Fact-checking is the process of verifying the authenticity of a claim with the help of evidence documents that either support or refute the claim, where a claim is defined as a factual statement subjected to verification [1]- [5]. Initial studies [6]- [13] on fact-checking primarily concentrated on curating datasets and developing methodologies for verifying claims related to politics, current affairs, newscast and discussions on social media. Scientific claims are grounded in empirical data derived from scientific studies and reports, whereas ordinary claims often express opinions or assertions about potential benefits or courses of action. However, verifying scientific claims poses * Equal contributions unique challenges in dataset curation and model development. Political and general claims can be easily fact-checked by general annotators or journalists, with numerous fact-checking websites available for such claims. In contrast, dedicated fact-checking platforms for scientific claims are scarce, and verifying these claims requires annotators with substantial domain expertise [14]. Given these unique challenges in scientific claim verification, the study [14] proposes a scientific claim verification dataset SCIFACT by manually constructing scientific claims derived from research paper abstracts, paired with abstracts of research papers that either support or refute the corresponding claim. Similarly, study [15] introduces SCIFACT-OPEN dataset for scientific claim verification by compiling pairs of scientific claims and abstracts of multiple research papers that either support or refute the scientific claim. 

Further, the work [16] proposes two methods for curating scientific claim verification datasets in the biomedical domain, namely Knowledge Base Informed Negations and CLAIMGEN-BART. The CLAIMGEN-BART method initially extracts the citation, along with the preceding and subsequent sentences, from a given research paper. Next, they encode these extracted sentences using the BART encoder and pass them to the BART decoder to generate a scientific claim supported by the research paper. In contrast, the Knowledge Base Informed Negations method replaces the named entity in a scientific claim, which is supported by the research paper to generate a scientific claim that is refuted by the research paper. However, the existing datasets for scientific claim verification exhibit several notable limitations.
</snippet>

Title: Can Large Language Models Detect Misinformation in Scientific News Reporting?
Snippet: Scientific information is communicated to the non-expert audience via popular press (news articles) and online platforms like blogs, social media posts, etc. Studies have shown that news with scientific-sounding content is trusted more than other types [33]. Therefore, any misinformation in the scientific domain can cause significant public risk as was evidenced during the recent COVID-19 pandemic [21]. Other examples include the emergence of vaccination hesitancy [3,29], eroded trust in health institutions [30], and the amplification of public fear and anxiety [23,39]. Therefore, it is imperative to identify misinformation in scientific news reporting. 

Several websites are maintained by science reporters (Health News Review 3 ) and scientists (Science Feedback 4 ) to track scientific misinformation in the media. Although such manual debunking is important, the sheer volume of scientific news can make this task unscalable. Natural language processing (NLP) based approaches have consequently started to emerge to deal with this problem. These methods typically involve language analysis, like detecting exaggeration [50] and certainty [24] and fact-checking [14] and claim verification [26]. Several claim verification datasets have also been developed for this problem [38,45] and a method for modeling information change from scientific article to scientific reporting has also been proposed [52]. 

While these works have laid the foundation to address this problem, the area is still in its nascence. Several challenges remain unaddressed: 1) there are no existing taxonomies to define dimensions of the scientific validity of scientific news articles that can be used in automated methods to detect misinformation in scientific news; 2) all existing datasets for scientific fact-checking relies on explicit claim generation from the news articles before it can be compared to the scientific articles for misinformation detection. This can be a cumbersome process in real-life scenarios where it would be potentially necessary for expert human involvement to first generate claims from the scientific article and 3) there is no generalized architecture that can detect scientific misinformation without an explicit claim generation step.
</snippet>

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: In the literature, studies [17], [18] briefly review and analyze the datasets and methodologies related to fact-checking. In litrature several datasets have been proposed to support general fact-checking research across various domains, including politics, journalism, and social media [1]- [3], [19]- [28]. Scientific fact-checking, a subfield of fact-checking, focuses on verifying claims about scientific knowledge, thereby combating misinformation while also supporting scientific inquiry, interpretation and public understanding of research [17]. Initial study [14] on scientific fact-checking proposed the SCIFACT dataset for scientific claim verification, using citance as claims and research abstracts as evidence. In contrast, SCIFACT-OPEN [15] extends the study [14] by collecting abstracts from multiple papers to support or refute the claims. Further study [16] introduced an encoder-decoder model that utilizes sentences surrounding stances and BART to generate claims supported by scientific evidence, with negative claims through named entity replacements to generate the claim refuted for scientific evidence. However, existing scientific claim verification datasets in the litrature have several key limitations. A primary concern is their limited size, as they typically consist of only a few hundred or thousand samples. This is inadequate for training models that can generalize effectively across diverse categories and domains [17]. Moreover, these datasets primarily depend on research paper abstracts as external evidence. However, abstracts offer only a concise summary and often lack the comprehensive details necessary for rigorous scientific claim verification [17]. Another limitation is the emphasis on extracting claims solely from sentences containing citations of research papers, which overlooks significant claims and insights presented in the results, discussion, and conclusion sections. Furthermore, there is the absence of a scientific claim verification dataset in the literature, which contains scientific claims and scientific evidence involving cardinal or numeral values to train models for numeral-aware scientific claim verifications. Motivated by such limitations with existing datasets for scientific claim verification in literature, this study proposes two novel datasets for scientific claim verification tasks SciCliamHunt and SciClaimHunt Num.
</snippet>

On the other hand, despite misinformation circulating online exceeding the capacity of manual fact-checking, traditional news outlets are skeptical towards adopting fully-automated methods [52].

Our work focuses on scientific claims in news articles and social media postings. For example, the sentence "Ibuprofen can worsen COVID-19 symptoms" is a scientific claim because it involves two scientific entities (Ibuprofen and COVID-19) and implies a causal relation between them. Grouping similar claims and linking them to related scientific literature is a complex task, to a large extent because of the different nature of the items that we are seeking to connect (i.e., social media postings, news articles, and scientific papers).

Title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Snippet: In this work, we introduced a new test collection, SCIFACT-OPEN, to support performance evaluation for open-domain scientific claim verification. The construction of SCIFACT-OPEN was enabled by our adaptation of the pooling strategy from IR for identification and annotation of evidence from a corpus of 500K documents. We hope such methodology can see further usage on other NLP tasks for which exhaustive annotation is infeasible. 

In analyzing the evidence in SCIFACT-OPEN ( §3.3), we found that some claims possess a large amount of conflicting evidence, and that evidence may not always match the specificity of the claims as written. We consider two future directions to improve the expressiveness of scientific claim verification. 

(1) As discussed in §3.3, one could still require systems to label each ECAP, but also to generate a revised claim matching the specificity of each evidence abstract. This output would provide users with fine-grained information indicating the conditions under which an input claim is likely to hold. We release 91 claim revisions, which can be used to facilitate exploratory research in this direction. 

(2) One could use the evidence identified by a claim verification system as input into a summarization system (DeYoung et al., 2021;Wallace et al., 2021) -potentially using additional quality criteria (e.g. citation count, publication venue) to filter or re-weight the articles included in the summary. This approach has the benefit of providing a concise summary to the user, but there is a greater risk of hallucination (Maynez et al., 2020). Overall, our analysis indicates that evaluations using SCIFACT-OPEN can provide key insights into modeling challenges associated with scientific claim verification. In particular, the performance of existing models declines substantially when evaluated on SCIFACT-OPEN, suggesting that current claim verification systems are not yet ready for deployment at scale. It is our hope that the dataset and analyses presented in this work will facilitate future modeling improvements, and lead to substantial new understanding of the scientific claim verification task.
</snippet>

Title: SciClaims: An End-to-End Generative System for Biomedical Claim Analysis
Snippet: We use SciFact, a benchmark dataset focused on biomedical literature, to evaluate SciClaims. It includes 1,400 expert-authored scientific claims, each linked to evidence-containing abstracts and annotated with a verification label. 

SciFact supports two complementary evaluations: (1) claim extraction, by comparing systemgenerated claims to human-written ones using shared source documents, and (2) claim verification, by assessing how accurately the system labels claim-evidence pairs.
</snippet>

Title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Snippet: In this section, we describe the construction of SCIFACT-OPEN. We report the performance of claim verification models on SCIFACT-OPEN in §4, and perform reliability checks on the results in §5. 

Our goal is to construct a test collection which can be used to assess the performance of claim verification systems deployed on a large corpus of scientific literature. This requires a collection of claims, a corpus of abstracts against which to verify them, and evidence annotations with which to evaluate system predictions. We use the claims from the SCIFACT-ORIG test set as our claims for SCIFACT-OPEN.2 To obtain evidence annotations, we use all evidence from SCIFACT-ORIG as evidence in our new dataset and collect additional evidence from the SCIFACT-OPEN corpus. 

For our corpus, we filter the S2ORC dataset (Lo et al., 2020) for all articles which (1) cover topics related to medicine or biology and (2) have at least one inbound and one outbound citation. From the roughly 6.5 million articles that pass these filters, we randomly sample 500K articles to form the corpus for SCIFACT-OPEN, making sure to include the 5K abstracts from SCIFACT-ORIG. We choose to limit the corpus to 500K abstracts to ensure that we can achieve sufficient annotation coverage of the available evidence. Additional details on corpus construction can be found in Appendix A. 

Unlike SCIFACT-ORIG (which is skewed toward highly-cited articles from "high-impact" journals), we do not impose any additional quality filters on articles included in SCIFACT-OPEN; thus, our corpus captures the full diversity of information likely to be encountered when scientific fact-checking systems are deployed on real-world resources like S2ORC, arXiv, 3 or PubMed Central. 4

Title: SciClops: Detecting and Contextualizing Scientific Claims for Assisting Manual Fact-Checking
Snippet: Grouping similar claims and linking them to related scientific literature is a complex task, to a large extent because of the different nature of the items that we are seeking to connect (i.e., social media postings, news articles, and scientific papers). These contain key passages that determine such connections, but are fundamentally different in terms of: i) verbosity, ranging from character-limited postings to extended scientific papers, and ii) complexity, ranging from a "social media friendly" style of writing to the more formal registry of journalism and academic writing. 

Finally, since there is a plethora of controversial claims (especially in the times of a pandemic), there is a need for a checkworthiness ranking that considers the prevalence and the reliability of the broadcasting medium. Providing a scientific context enables non-expert fact-checkers to verify claims with more precision than commercial fact-checking systems, and more confidence since the provided context is fully-interpretable (details in §6.3). 

Our Contribution. In this paper we describe SciClops (Figure 1), a method to assist manual verification of dubious claims, in scientific fields with open-access literature and limited fact-checking coverage. The technical contributions we introduce are the following: 

• pretrained and fine-tuned transformer-based models for scientific claim extraction from news and social media ( §3); • multimodal, joint clustering models for claims and papers that utilize both content and graph information ( §4); • methods for ranking check-worthy claims using a custom knowledge graph, and methods for creating enhanced scientific contexts to assist manual fact-checking ( §5); and • extensive experiments involving expert and non-expert users, strong baselines and commercial fact-checking systems ( §6).
</snippet>

Title: Two Contrasting Data Annotation Paradigms for Subjective NLP Tasks
Snippet: Three types of data are available to train scientific claim verification systems. (1) In-domain fact-checking annotations are the "gold standard", but they are expensive to create and require expert annotators.

(2) General-domain fact-checking datasets like FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) are abundantly available, but generalize poorly to scientific claims (see §6.1). (3) Scientific documents -either unlabeled or labeled for different tasks -are abundant, and high precision heuristics (described in §4.2) can be used to generate document-level fact-checking labels y(c, a) for these data.

We train MULTIVERS as follows: we first pretrain on a combination of general-domain factchecking annotations, combined with weaklylabeled in-domain data. 5 Then, we finetune on the target scientific fact-checking dataset. The multitask architecture of MULTIVERS is well-suited to this strategy, since the model can be trained on data with or without rationale annotations. When no rationales are available, we set λ rationale = 0 in the loss function and train as usual. By contrast, training an "extract-then-label" model on weaklysupervised data requires creating rationale annotations R(c, a), which is quite noisy (see §4.2).
</snippet>

Title: Claim Extraction in Biomedical Publications using Deep Discourse Model and Transfer Learning
Snippet: Claims are a fundamental unit of scientific discourse. However, the exponential growth of publications has made it challenging for researchers to keep track of research papers introducing new claims. Automatic extraction of claims from scientific articles promises to alleviate some of these problems, additionally supporting other scientific processes such as knowledge exploration, efficient reading [1], and automated text summarization [2]. DARPA's recently launched Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program to tackle automatic claim detection (with confidence measurement) underscores the importance of the task in wider contexts. sentence is either from background, introduction, method, result, or conclusion sections. However, the annotated dataset related to scientific domain is still limited as presented in [4,5,6]. Since claim extraction and discourse tagging are related, it creates an opportunity for applying techniques that exploit weak supervision and transfer learning [7]. 

In this paper, we introduce a scientific claim detection task with a dataset of 1,500 scientific papers with expertly annotated claims. This is the largest claim-annotated dataset specifically aimed towards scientific documents. We build on a neural discourse tagging model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) with Conditional Random Field (CRF) [8] and transfer the representations to train a claim extraction model. Our fine-tuned model achieves 47% higher F1-score compared to the rule-based method presented in the previous research [5]. We show that pre-training the model on the Pubmed-RCT dataset allows our model to achieve 14% higher F1-score than a model trained solely on the claim extraction dataset. We make the code for claim extraction, our dataset, and our annotation tool publicly available to the community1 .
</snippet>

Title: Table-Text Alignment: Explaining Claim Verification Against Tables in Scientific Papers
Snippet: During annotation, we observed frequent edge cases where claim verification was hindered by poor table formatting, unclear language, or missing context. We propose a taxonomy of five ambiguity types based on annotator notes and discussion: (iv) Subjective Adjectives: Use of vague or nonquantifiable terms (e.g., "poor", "substantial", or "a large margin"). 

(v) Unclear Claims: Ambiguous references to table elements (e.g., "this model", "these scores"). 

We provide examples for each case in Appendix A. We hope this taxonomy will guide future dataset development and improve robustness in scientific claim verification tasks.
</snippet>

Below is a practical, evidence‑backed guide to choosing between naturally‑occurring claims (from science news/social media or press releases) and expert‑written claims (curated or model‑generated with expert review) for scientific fact‑verification datasets.

Summary
- Use naturally‑occurring claims when you need out‑of‑the‑wild coverage, trustworthiness auditing of media narratives, and training robustness via realistic ambiguity and prior‑knowledge dependence; build safeguards for interpretability and safety since these claims can be trusted more by the public and often embed informal language and imprecision. <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Scientific information conveyed via news and social platforms is trusted more by non‑expert audiences, and misinformation in this domain can cause significant public risk; manual debunking by scientists and journalists is necessary but unscalable</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Connecting social‑media/news claims to scientific papers is hard because of differences in verbosity and complexity; providing scientific context improves precision and confidence for non‑expert fact‑checkers</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-0">Science releases and articles can contain significant exaggeration and misinformation; automated systems are needed to judge veracity and credibility</cite>.
- Use expert‑written claims when you need precise, interpretable veracity targets with linked evidence, controlled difficulty distributions, and generalization to research‑paper content; expert‑written claim+evidence pairs (e.g., SciFact) and expert curation pipelines improve reliability and expose numeric/conditional specificity issues. <cite id="0f4af27c-0">SCIFACT uses expert‑written claims paired with paper abstracts, but abstracts often lack details needed for rigorous verification</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">In SCIFACT‑OPEN, some claims have conflicting or specificity‑mismatching evidence; models’ performance declines substantially on this open‑corpus setting</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-2">SciFact includes 1,400 expert‑authored claims with evidence‑linked labels enabling extraction and verification evaluations</cite>.

1) Clarify goals and constraints
- If your goal is to audit and counteract misinformation in public scientific communication, naturally‑occurring claims from news/social media are essential to measure real user exposure and trust calibration. <cite id="e5449d2b-2">News with scientific‑sounding content is trusted more than other types; misinformation in scientific news contributed to vaccination hesitancy and eroded trust in institutions during COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-0">Media releases and articles can contain substantial exaggeration; automated systems can help readers separate verified facts from speculation or falsehoods</cite>.
- If your goal is to benchmark model understanding of scientific evidence and produce interpretable rationales, expert‑written claims with linked evidence enable precise evaluation and error analysis. <cite id="0f4af27c-2">SciFact evaluates both claim extraction (matching system‑generated to human‑written claims) and claim verification (labeling claim–evidence pairs)</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">SCIFACT‑OPEN’s analysis reveals conflicting evidence and specificity mismatches, motivating outputs that revise claims to conditions under which they hold</cite>.

2) When to use naturally‑occurring claims (news/social or “science releases”)
- To capture what the public actually encounters and builds beliefs from: social media, blogs, and news posts often summarize or reframe research in ways that introduce exaggeration, uncertainty shifts, or omitted context. <cite id="e5449d2b-0">Estimates reported in 2014 found 40% of science press releases contained exaggerated advice and 33% exaggerated claims; similar issues persist in social media</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Science communicators and scientists maintain debunking resources, but volume makes manual checking unscalable</cite>.
- To stress‑test retrieval and veracity prediction under ambiguity and prior‑knowledge dependence: naturally‑occurring claims exhibit informal language, subjective adjectives, and unclear references that degrade model accuracy and reveal failure modes. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Social media and news claims differ in verbosity and complexity from scientific literature; clustering and enhanced contexts are needed to link claims to papers</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-3">Annotators frequently hit edge cases from poor formatting, unclear language, or missing context; a taxonomy of ambiguities includes vague adjectives and unclear references</cite>.
- To build checkworthiness and interpretability tools that assist non‑experts: datasets and systems that present scientific contexts improve precision and confidence compared to black‑box outputs. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Providing scientific contexts enables non‑experts to verify claims with more precision than commercial systems and with greater confidence due to fully interpretable context</cite>.
- Caveats: raw news/social claims require careful handling to avoid propagating media distortions and to maintain journalistic trust. <cite id="e5449d2b-4">Traditional media are skeptical of fully automated fact‑checking because evidence can be poorly interpretable; automation should assist rather than replace human validation</cite>.

Practical guidance when choosing naturally‑occurring claims:
- Prefer claims with explicit numeric/conditional content where possible, and pair them with retrievable paper evidence; otherwise, models can hallucinate precise numbers or conditions. <cite id="0f4af27c-3">SCIFACT requires systems to retrieve relevant sentences from abstracts and decide support/refute status for expert‑written claims</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-0">Abstracts are concise summaries that often lack comprehensive details; claims outside citation sentences are overlooked</cite>.
- Add provenance metadata (publisher, date, sentiment/persuasiveness) and require explainable rationales pointing to specific passages; evaluate checkworthiness ranking by prevalence and reliability. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">There is a need for checkworthiness ranking considering prevalence and reliability of the broadcasting medium; clustering and ranking methods assist manual verification</cite>.

3) When to use expert‑written claims (curated or model‑generated with expert review)
- When you need reliable, interpretable ground truth: expert‑authored claim–evidence pairs (e.g., SciFact) provide clear labels and traceable passages, enabling robust extraction/verification pipelines and error analyses. <cite id="0f4af27c-2">SciFact includes 1,400 expert‑authored claims linked to evidence‑containing abstracts and verification labels for end‑to‑end evaluation</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-3">SCIFACT has emerged as a popular benchmark for scientific fact verification</cite>.
- When generalizing to open‑domain settings: expert‑written claims can seed models that scale to large literature corpora, but performance drops when evidence is abundant and conflicting, underscoring the need for revision and summarization with safeguards. <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Performance declines substantially on SCIFACT‑OPEN; conflicting evidence and specificity mismatches are common, motivating claim revisions and quality‑aware summarization with risks of hallucination</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-4">SCIFACT‑OPEN samples 500K articles to capture diversity like S2ORC/arXiv/PubMed Central, without additional quality filters beyond topic and citation criteria</cite>.
- When training end‑to‑end systems: expert‑written scientific claims facilitate joint optimization of claim extraction and verification; data generation frameworks can augment coverage while maintaining expert oversight. <cite id="0f4af27c-2">SciClaims evaluates extraction by comparing system‑generated to human‑written claims under shared source documents</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-1">Methods like CLAIMGEN‑BART extract sentence contexts to generate supported claims and use named‑entity replacement to generate refuted claims; existing datasets have key limitations</cite>.
- Caveats: abstract‑only evidence and claim selection from citation sentences can miss nuance; expert curation should also sample results/discussion and include numeric claims. <cite id="0f4af27c-0">Abstracts often lack comprehensive details; emphasis on claims with citations overlooks results, discussion, and conclusions; datasets lacking cardinal‑value claims hinder numeral‑aware verification</cite>.

4) Hybrid and data‑program strategies
- Combine both provenances: use expert‑written claims to teach core scientific reasoning and retrieval, then evaluate and harden models on naturally‑occurring news/social claims to ensure robustness and checkworthiness under real‑world ambiguity. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Assisting manual verification with claim clustering and enhanced scientific contexts improves precision and confidence, bridging expert and non‑expert workflows</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Automated methods for detecting exaggeration, certainty, and fact‑checking in scientific news are emerging due to scalability limits of manual debunking</cite>.
- Use expert‑assisted generation pipelines for news/social claims: extract candidate claims, re‑phrase/standardize them, and link to paper evidence; add numeric normalization and condition extraction to reduce ambiguity. <cite id="d05ab01d-3">Ambiguity types like vague adjectives and unclear references motivate taxonomy‑guided dataset development and robust models</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-1">CLAIMGEN‑BART encodes surrounding sentences to generate supported claims and uses entity replacement for refuted claims, enabling curated scientific claim sets</cite>.
- Ensure interpretability and safety: require passage‑level rationales, provenance, and confidence bands; adopt checkworthiness ranking that penalizes high‑risk, high‑prevalence claims. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Enhanced scientific contexts enable interpretable evidence for non‑experts; checkworthiness ranking by prevalence and reliability is recommended</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-4">Traditional media caution that poorly interpretable automated evidence can damage reputation; automation should assist rather than replace</cite>.

5) Risks and mitigations
- Risks of naturally‑occurring claims: public trust and uptake depend on accuracy; misinformation in news/social media can drive hesitancy and fear. <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Misinformation in scientific news raised vaccination hesitancy and eroded trust; science reporters and scientists maintain debunking sites but cannot keep pace</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-0">Exaggeration and misinformation in “science releases” and articles are persistent</cite>.
  Mitigations: enforce evidence traceability, require uncertainty handling, and include domain experts and non‑experts in evaluation. <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Providing interpretable scientific contexts improves precision and confidence for non‑experts, enabling assisted manual fact‑checking</cite>.
- Risks of expert‑written claims: abstract‑only evidence and narrow selection can mislead, especially for numeric/conditional claims; models may overfit to curated distributions. <cite id="0f4af27c-0">Abstracts lack comprehensive details; claims outside citation sentences are overlooked; cardinal‑value claims are underrepresented</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Conflicting evidence and specificity mismatches degrade accuracy; revision and quality‑aware summarization are needed with hallucination risks</cite>.
  Mitigations: scale to full corpora (S2ORC/arXiv/PubMed Central), include numeric/conditional claims, and require claim revision/summarization with quality criteria and uncertainty. <cite id="0f4af27c-4">Sampling 500K articles across medicine/biology with inbound/outbound citations captures real‑world diversity like S2ORC/arXiv/PMC</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Release claim revisions and propose summarization with quality filters to indicate conditions under which claims hold</cite>.

6) Practical recommendations by scenario
- Auditing public scientific communication: predominantly use naturally‑occurring claims from reputable outlets and social platforms, with expert review to triage and revise claims, and to deliver interpretable, source‑linked counter‑explanations. <cite id="e5449d2b-2">News platforms drive trust and misinformation risk; automation complements manual debunking but must be interpretable</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Scientific contexts and clustering improve precision and confidence for non‑expert checkers</cite>.
- Building scientific reasoning baselines: start with expert‑written claim–evidence pairs (e.g., SciFact) to train extraction and verification; progressively transfer to news/social claims to evaluate robustness and deploy checkworthiness ranking. <cite id="0f4af27c-2">SciFact provides expert‑authored claims linked to evidence and supports extraction and verification evaluations</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Assisted manual verification with enhanced contexts improves performance over black‑box systems</cite>.
- Domain expansion and numeric reasoning: include expert‑curated numeric/conditional claims and teach models to revise claims to reflect evidence specificity; then test on naturally‑occurring claims that often lack numbers or misuse uncertainty. <cite id="0f4af27c-0">Expert datasets often lack numeral‑aware examples, overlooking results/discussion; this hinders verification of numeric claims</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-3">Ambiguity from subjective adjectives and unclear references is frequent and taxonomizable</cite>.
- Safety and interpretability in deployment: require passage‑level rationales with provenance, avoid unreviewed model‑generated summaries, and adopt editorial oversight for high‑prevalence claims. <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Summarization can concisely present evidence but risks hallucination; propose quality criteria (e.g., citation count) to filter summaries</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-4">Traditional media emphasize that interpretable evidence is essential; automation should assist human validation</cite>.

7) Dataset design patterns you can adopt
- News/social media tracklist: curate claim sets from science reporting pages; add provenance (URL, outlet, sentiment), normalize claims, link to supporting/contrasting papers; require annotators to mark certainty, conflicts, and missing context. <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Science misinformation in news poses large public risk; manual debunking is unscalable, driving NLP approaches to detect exaggeration, certainty, and fact‑check</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Clustering claims with papers and ranking check‑worthiness by prevalence/reliability improves assisted manual fact‑checking</cite>.
- Expert‑curated scientific tracklist: compile claim–evidence pairs from abstracts and full texts; include positive, negative, and “not enough info” categories; add numeric/conditional variants; expose claim revisions when evidence conflicts. <cite id="0f4af27c-0">SCIFACT uses citation‑derived claims and abstracts as evidence but misses details in results/discussion; cardinal claims are underrepresented</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Conflicting evidence and specificity mismatches are common; releasing revisions helps users understand conditions under which claims hold</cite>.
- Generation‑plus‑review pipeline: extract candidate claims from social/news and scientific documents; use encoder–decoder or rule‑based heuristics to generate crisp, numeric‑aware claims; route to expert or LLM‑plus‑expert review; bundle with evidence spans and uncertainty categories. <cite id="e5449d2b-1">CLAIMGEN‑BART encodes surrounding sentences to generate supported claims and uses entity replacement for refuted claims</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-3">Ambiguity taxonomies (subjective adjectives, unclear references) guide robust dataset development</cite>.
- Open‑corpus evaluation: measure retrieval and veracity under large, heterogeneous corpora (S2ORC/arXiv/PMC) to stress generalization; include checkworthiness metrics and user studies with experts and non‑experts. <cite id="0f4af27c-4">SCIFACT‑OPEN samples 500K articles to mirror real‑world resources like S2ORC, arXiv, and PubMed Central</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">User studies show enhanced contexts improve precision and confidence for non‑experts</cite>.

Bottom line: Prefer expert‑written claims when you need precise, interpretable, and generalizable evaluation targets linked to scientific evidence; use naturally‑occurring claims when you need realistic, high‑stakes coverage of public discourse and to build robust, checkworthiness‑aware systems. In practice, combine both with expert‑assisted generation and review, add numeric/conditional coverage, and enforce interpretable, provenanced rationales to balance scientific validity with real‑world applicability. <cite id="0f4af27c-2">Expert‑authored claim–evidence pairs enable extraction and verification evaluations</cite> <cite id="0f4af27c-1">Performance degrades in open corpora with conflicting evidence, motivating claim revision and quality‑aware summarization</cite> <cite id="e5449d2b-2">Naturally‑occurring scientific news claims carry outsized public trust and risk, necessitating scalable, interpretable verification</cite> <cite id="d05ab01d-0">Providing scientific contexts improves precision and confidence for assisted manual fact‑checking</cite>.</answer>

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: Fact-checking plays a vital role in information validation, serving as a crucial defence against the widespread dissemination of misinformation and disinformation. Fact-checking is the process of verifying the authenticity of a claim with the help of evidence documents that either support or refute the claim, where a claim is defined as a factual statement subjected to verification [1]- [5]. Initial studies [6]- [13] on fact-checking primarily concentrated on curating datasets and developing methodologies for verifying claims related to politics, current affairs, newscast and discussions on social media. Scientific claims are grounded in empirical data derived from scientific studies and reports, whereas ordinary claims often express opinions or assertions about potential benefits or courses of action. However, verifying scientific claims poses * Equal contributions unique challenges in dataset curation and model development. Political and general claims can be easily fact-checked by general annotators or journalists, with numerous fact-checking websites available for such claims. In contrast, dedicated fact-checking platforms for scientific claims are scarce, and verifying these claims requires annotators with substantial domain expertise [14]. Given these unique challenges in scientific claim verification, the study [14] proposes a scientific claim verification dataset SCIFACT by manually constructing scientific claims derived from research paper abstracts, paired with abstracts of research papers that either support or refute the corresponding claim. Similarly, study [15] introduces SCIFACT-OPEN dataset for scientific claim verification by compiling pairs of scientific claims and abstracts of multiple research papers that either support or refute the scientific claim. 

Further, the work [16] proposes two methods for curating scientific claim verification datasets in the biomedical domain, namely Knowledge Base Informed Negations and CLAIMGEN-BART. Title: Can Large Language Models Detect Misinformation in Scientific News Reporting?
Snippet: Scientific information is communicated to the non-expert audience via popular press (news articles) and online platforms like blogs, social media posts, etc. Studies have shown that news with scientific-sounding content is trusted more than other types [33]. Therefore, any misinformation in the scientific domain can cause significant public risk as was evidenced during the recent COVID-19 pandemic [21]. Other examples include the emergence of vaccination hesitancy [3,29], eroded trust in health institutions [30], and the amplification of public fear and anxiety [23,39]. Therefore, it is imperative to identify misinformation in scientific news reporting. 

Several websites are maintained by science reporters (Health News Review 3 ) and scientists (Science Feedback 4 ) to track scientific misinformation in the media. Although such manual debunking is important, the sheer volume of scientific news can make this task unscalable. Natural language processing (NLP) based approaches have consequently started to emerge to deal with this problem. These methods typically involve language analysis, like detecting exaggeration [50] and certainty [24] and fact-checking [14] and claim verification [26]. Several claim verification datasets have also been developed for this problem [38,45] and a method for modeling information change from scientific article to scientific reporting has also been proposed [52]. 

While these works have laid the foundation to address this problem, the area is still in its nascence. Several challenges remain unaddressed: 1) there are no existing taxonomies to define dimensions of the scientific validity of scientific news articles that can be used in automated methods to detect misinformation in scientific news; 2) all existing datasets for scientific fact-checking relies on explicit claim generation from the news articles before it can be compared to the scientific articles for misinformation detection. This can be a cumbersome process in real-life scenarios where it would be potentially necessary for expert human involvement to first generate claims from the scientific article and 3) there is no generalized architecture that can detect scientific misinformation without an explicit claim generation step.

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: In the literature, studies [17], [18] briefly review and analyze the datasets and methodologies related to fact-checking. In litrature several datasets have been proposed to support general fact-checking research across various domains, including politics, journalism, and social media [1]- [3], [19]- [28]. Scientific fact-checking, a subfield of fact-checking, focuses on verifying claims about scientific knowledge, thereby combating misinformation while also supporting scientific inquiry, interpretation and public understanding of research [17]. Initial study [14] on scientific fact-checking proposed the SCIFACT dataset for scientific claim verification, using citance as claims and research abstracts as evidence. In contrast, SCIFACT-OPEN [15] extends the study [14] by collecting abstracts from multiple papers to support or refute the claims. Further study [16] introduced an encoder-decoder model that utilizes sentences surrounding stances and BART to generate claims supported by scientific evidence, with negative claims through named entity replacements to generate the claim refuted for scientific evidence. However, existing scientific claim verification datasets in the litrature have several key limitations. A primary concern is their limited size, as they typically consist of only a few hundred or thousand samples. This is inadequate for training models that can generalize effectively across diverse categories and domains [17]. Moreover, these datasets primarily depend on research paper abstracts as external evidence. However, abstracts offer only a concise summary and often lack the comprehensive details necessary for rigorous scientific claim verification [17]. Another limitation is the emphasis on extracting claims solely from sentences containing citations of research papers, which overlooks significant claims and insights presented in the results, discussion, and conclusion sections. Furthermore, there is the absence of a scientific claim verification dataset in the literature, which contains scientific claims and scientific evidence involving cardinal or numeral values to train models for numeral-aware scientific claim verifications. Motivated by such limitations with existing datasets for scientific claim verification in literature, this study proposes two novel datasets for scientific claim verification tasks SciCliamHunt and SciClaimHunt Num.

Title: SciClops: Detecting and Contextualizing Scientific Claims for Assisting Manual Fact-Checking
Snippet: [ 3 7 ] G a d -E lr a b e t a l. [ 1 6 ] C h e n e t a l. [ 7 ] SciClops 

On the other hand, despite misinformation circulating online exceeding the capacity of manual fact-checking, traditional news outlets are skeptical towards adopting fully-automated methods [52]. 

Their main concern is that such tools provide poorly-interpretable evidence (according to the journalistic standards), and any false judgment can lead to a downfall of the outlet's reputation. Indeed, even big tech companies were forced to suspend automated factchecking features due to similar criticism from news outlets [15]. Hence, the consensus regarding the usage of automation in journalism is that it should assist but not replace journalists and news consumers when they validate the veracity of news, enabling the movement onward the era of citizen journalism [38]. 

Our work focuses on scientific claims in news articles and social media postings. As scientific claims, we consider sentence-level segments that involve one or more scientific entities and are eligible for fact-checking. For example, the sentence "Ibuprofen can worsen COVID-19 symptoms" is a scientific claim because it involves two scientific entities (Ibuprofen and COVID-19) and implies a causal relation between them. To increase the coverage of our definition, we bound neither the number of entities nor the type of relation between them. Such non-deterministic definition makes the detection of scientific claims a challenging task, even for human annotators (details in §6.1). To address this task and enable the discovery of complex-structured claims, there is a need for advanced language models which are fine-tuned with domain-specific knowledge. 

Once we identify candidate scientific claims, we seek evidence that proves or contradicts them via contextualization, i.e., via building an enhanced context of trustworthy information. In the scientific domain, the appropriate context consists of related scientific papers. Grouping similar claims and linking them to related scientific literature is a complex task, to a large extent because of the different nature of the items that we are seeking to connect (i.e., social media postings, news articles, and scientific papers).

Title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Snippet: In this work, we introduced a new test collection, SCIFACT-OPEN, to support performance evaluation for open-domain scientific claim verification. The construction of SCIFACT-OPEN was enabled by our adaptation of the pooling strategy from IR for identification and annotation of evidence from a corpus of 500K documents. We hope such methodology can see further usage on other NLP tasks for which exhaustive annotation is infeasible. 

In analyzing the evidence in SCIFACT-OPEN ( §3.3), we found that some claims possess a large amount of conflicting evidence, and that evidence may not always match the specificity of the claims as written. We consider two future directions to improve the expressiveness of scientific claim verification. 

(1) As discussed in §3.3, one could still require systems to label each ECAP, but also to generate a revised claim matching the specificity of each evidence abstract. This output would provide users with fine-grained information indicating the conditions under which an input claim is likely to hold. We release 91 claim revisions, which can be used to facilitate exploratory research in this direction. 

(2) One could use the evidence identified by a claim verification system as input into a summarization system (DeYoung et al., 2021;Wallace et al., 2021) -potentially using additional quality criteria (e.g. citation count, publication venue) to filter or re-weight the articles included in the summary. This approach has the benefit of providing a concise summary to the user, but there is a greater risk of hallucination (Maynez et al., 2020). Overall, our analysis indicates that evaluations using SCIFACT-OPEN can provide key insights into modeling challenges associated with scientific claim verification. In particular, the performance of existing models declines substantially when evaluated on SCIFACT-OPEN, suggesting that current claim verification systems are not yet ready for deployment at scale. It is our hope that the dataset and analyses presented in this work will facilitate future modeling improvements, and lead to substantial new understanding of the scientific claim verification task.

Title: SciClaims: An End-to-End Generative System for Biomedical Claim Analysis
Snippet: We use SciFact, a benchmark dataset focused on biomedical literature, to evaluate SciClaims. It includes 1,400 expert-authored scientific claims, each linked to evidence-containing abstracts and annotated with a verification label. 

SciFact supports two complementary evaluations: (1) claim extraction, by comparing systemgenerated claims to human-written ones using shared source documents, and (2) claim verification, by assessing how accurately the system labels claim-evidence pairs.

Title: Synthetic Disinformation Attacks on Automated Fact Verification Systems
Snippet: We briefly describe the provenance and structure of our studied datasets and refer the reader to the original works for in-depth descriptions of the construction of these resources. snippet.text:
In this work, we introduced a new test collection, SCIFACT-OPEN, to support performance evaluation for open-domain scientific claim verification. The construction of SCIFACT-OPEN was enabled by our adaptation of the pooling strategy from IR for identification and annotation of evidence from a corpus of 500K documents. We hope such methodology can see further usage on other NLP tasks for which exhaustive annotation is infeasible. 

In analyzing the evidence in SCIFACT-OPEN ( §3.3), we found that some claims possess a large amount of conflicting evidence, and that evidence may not always match the specificity of the claims as written. We consider two future directions to improve the expressiveness of scientific claim verification. 

(1) As discussed in §3.3, one could still require systems to label each ECAP, but also to generate a revised claim matching the specificity of each evidence abstract. This output would provide users with fine-grained information indicating the conditions under which an input claim is likely to hold. We release 91 claim revisions, which can be used to facilitate exploratory research in this direction. 

(2) One could use the evidence identified by a claim verification system as input into a summarization system (DeYoung et al., 2021;Wallace et al., 2021) -potentially using additional quality criteria (e.g. citation count, publication venue) to filter or re-weight the articles included in the summary. This approach has the benefit of providing a concise summary to the user, but there is a greater risk of hallucination (Maynez et al., 2020). Overall, our analysis indicates that evaluations using SCIFACT-OPEN can provide key insights into modeling challenges associated with scientific claim verification. In particular, the performance of existing models declines substantially when evaluated on SCIFACT-OPEN, suggesting that current claim verification systems are not yet ready for deployment at scale. It is our hope that the dataset and analyses presented in this work will facilitate future modeling improvements, and lead to substantial new understanding of the scientific claim verification task.

Title: SciClops: Detecting and Contextualizing Scientific Claims for Assisting Manual Fact-Checking
Snippet: Grouping similar claims and linking them to related scientific literature is a complex task, to a large extent because of the different nature of the items that we are seeking to connect (i.e., social media postings, news articles, and scientific papers). These contain key passages that determine such connections, but are fundamentally different in terms of: i) verbosity, ranging from character-limited postings to extended scientific papers, and ii) complexity, ranging from a "social media friendly" style of writing to the more formal registry of journalism and academic writing. 

Finally, since there is a plethora of controversial claims (especially in the times of a pandemic), there is a need for a checkworthiness ranking that considers the prevalence and the reliability of the broadcasting medium. Providing a scientific context enables non-expert fact-checkers to verify claims with more precision than commercial fact-checking systems, and more confidence since the provided context is fully-interpretable (details in §6.3). 

Our Contribution. In this paper we describe SciClops (Figure 1), a method to assist manual verification of dubious claims, in scientific fields with open-access literature and limited fact-checking coverage. The technical contributions we introduce are the following: 

• pretrained and fine-tuned transformer-based models for scientific claim extraction from news and social media ( §3); • multimodal, joint clustering models for claims and papers that utilize both content and graph information ( §4); • methods for ranking check-worthy claims using a custom knowledge graph, and methods for creating enhanced scientific contexts to assist manual fact-checking ( §5); and • extensive experiments involving expert and non-expert users, strong baselines and commercial fact-checking systems ( §6).

Title: Two Contrasting Data Annotation Paradigms for Subjective NLP Tasks
Snippet: Three types of data are available to train scientific claim verification systems. (1) In-domain fact-checking annotations are the "gold standard", but they are expensive to create and require expert annotators.

(2) General-domain fact-checking datasets like FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) are abundantly available, but generalize poorly to scientific claims (see §6.1). (3) Scientific documents -either unlabeled or labeled for different tasks -are abundant, and high precision heuristics (described in §4.2) can be used to generate document-level fact-checking labels y(c, a) for these data.

We train MULTIVERS as follows: we first pretrain on a combination of general-domain factchecking annotations, combined with weaklylabeled in-domain data. 5 Then, we finetune on the target scientific fact-checking dataset. The multitask architecture of MULTIVERS is well-suited to this strategy, since the model can be trained on data with or without rationale annotations. When no rationales are available, we set λ rationale = 0 in the loss function and train as usual. By contrast, training an "extract-then-label" model on weaklysupervised data requires creating rationale annotations R(c, a), which is quite noisy (see §4.2).

Title: Claim Extraction in Biomedical Publications using Deep Discourse Model and Transfer Learning
Snippet: Claims are a fundamental unit of scientific discourse. However, the exponential growth of publications has made it challenging for researchers to keep track of research papers introducing new claims. Automatic extraction of claims from scientific articles promises to alleviate some of these problems, additionally supporting other scientific processes such as knowledge exploration, efficient reading [1], and automated text summarization [2]. DARPA's recently launched Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program to tackle automatic claim detection (with confidence measurement) underscores the importance of the task in wider contexts. sentence is either from background, introduction, method, result, or conclusion sections. However, the annotated dataset related to scientific domain is still limited as presented in [4,5,6]. Since claim extraction and discourse tagging are related, it creates an opportunity for applying techniques that exploit weak supervision and transfer learning [7]. 

In this paper, we introduce a scientific claim detection task with a dataset of 1,500 scientific papers with expertly annotated claims. This is the largest claim-annotated dataset specifically aimed towards scientific documents. We build on a neural discourse tagging model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) with Conditional Random Field (CRF) [8] and transfer the representations to train a claim extraction model. Our fine-tuned model achieves 47% higher F1-score compared to the rule-based method presented in the previous research [5]. We show that pre-training the model on the Pubmed-RCT dataset allows our model to achieve 14% higher F1-score than a model trained solely on the claim extraction dataset. We make the code for claim extraction, our dataset, and our annotation tool publicly available to the community1 .

Title: Table-Text Alignment: Explaining Claim Verification Against Tables in Scientific Papers
Snippet: During annotation, we observed frequent edge cases where claim verification was hindered by poor table formatting, unclear language, or missing context. We propose a taxonomy of five ambiguity types based on annotator notes and discussion: (iv) Subjective Adjectives: Use of vague or nonquantifiable terms (e.g., "poor", "substantial", or "a large margin"). 

(v) Unclear Claims: Ambiguous references to table elements (e.g., "this model", "these scores"). 

We provide examples for each case in Appendix A. We hope this taxonomy will guide future dataset development and improve robustness in scientific claim verification tasks.

Claims are a fundamental unit of scientific discourse. However, the exponential growth of publications has made it challenging for researchers to keep track of research papers introducing new claims. Automatic extraction of claims from scientific articles promises to alleviate some of these problems, additionally supporting other scientific processes such as knowledge exploration, efficient reading [1], and automated text summarization [2]. DARPA's recently launched Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program to tackle automatic claim detection (with confidence measurement) underscores the importance of the task in wider contexts. sentence is either from background, introduction, method, result, or conclusion sections. However, the annotated dataset related to scientific domain is still limited as presented in [4,5,6]. Since claim extraction and discourse tagging are related, it creates an opportunity for applying techniques that exploit weak supervision and transfer learning [7]. 

In this paper, we introduce a scientific claim detection task with a dataset of 1,500 scientific papers with expertly annotated claims. This is the largest claim-annotated dataset specifically aimed towards scientific documents. We build on a neural discourse tagging model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) with Conditional Random Field (CRF) [8] and transfer the representations to train a claim extraction model. Our fine-tuned model achieves 47% higher F1-score compared to the rule-based method presented in the previous research [5]. We show that pre-training the model on the Pubmed-RCT dataset allows our model to achieve 14% higher F1-score than a model trained solely on the claim extraction dataset. We make the code for claim extraction, our dataset, and our annotation tool publicly available to the community1 .

documents.title: Table-Text Alignment: Explaining Claim Verification Against Tables in Scientific Papers
documents.snippet:
During annotation, we observed frequent edge cases where claim verification was hindered by poor table formatting, unclear language, or missing context. We propose a taxonomy of five ambiguity types based on annotator notes and discussion: (iv) Subjective Adjectives: Use of vague or nonquantifiable terms (e.g., "poor", "substantial", or "a large margin"). 

(v) Unclear Claims: Ambiguous references to table elements (e.g., "this model", "these scores"). 

We provide examples for each case in Appendix A. We hope this taxonomy will guide future dataset development and improve robustness in scientific claim verification tasks.

SCIFACT presents the challenge of understanding scientific writing as systems must retrieve relevant sentences from paper abstracts and identify if the sentences support or refute a presented scientific claim. It has emerged as a popular benchmark for evaluating scientific fact verification systems (Pradeep et al. 2021).

attempts.answer:
Summary

Across scientific fact-verification datasets, the number of reasoning steps needed to verify a claim typically falls into two regimes: a large majority of claims can be resolved with one or two evidence pieces (single- or shallow multi-hop), while a minority require deeper multi-hop chains (often 3–4 hops) that integrate multiple documents and relations; the proportion and depth of multi-hop reasoning vary systematically with dataset design and domain coverage. <cite id="b52c4464-0">In many public datasets, most claims require only a single piece of evidence, and multi-hop datasets can also contain shortcut biases that make single-path verification easy if not carefully controlled</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER explicitly stratifies claims into 2-, 3-, and 4-hop reasoning, reflecting a minority of deep multi-hop instances</cite>, and <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER likewise emphasizes primarily 2–3 hop reasoning over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>. Empirical analyses show that models often achieve peak accuracy at around two hops on simpler data like FEVER, indicating that many claims are verifiable with shallow chains, while multi-hop datasets require tuning to match the claim’s reasoning depth. <cite id="55e77ff1-3">SciFact-Open further shows an unequal allocation of evidence across claims, with a small fraction of well-studied, short, entity-rich claims consuming most evidence and likely requiring fewer steps</cite>.

What constitutes a “reasoning step”

In scientific claim verification, a “reasoning step” can be measured in several equivalent ways: number of evidence hops retrieved (query iterations linking entities and events across documents), number of integrated facts used to derive a logical conclusion, or depth of chain-of-thought linking premises to the claim. <cite id="b52c4464-3">Complex claims require iterative retrieval and logical integration over multiple entities, events, and causal relations, often implemented as stepwise retrieval where each query is generated from the claim and prior evidence to form a complete evidence set</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER formalizes this by grouping claims by the number of hops across passages</cite>, and <cite id="55e77ff1-4">HoVER is widely used to evaluate 4-hop reasoning</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER focuses on 2–3 hop chains over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>.

Distributions by dataset

- FEVER and FEVER-like sources (PubMed/Wikipedia): single-hop dominance with occasional multi-hop.
  <cite id="b52c4464-0">Prior work on FEVER found that most claims require only a single piece of evidence to verify, and models can exploit annotation artifacts or shortcut paths</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-4">Debiasing methods revealed that even multi-hop datasets can hide spurious correlations, and performance can drop when such shortcuts are removed</cite>. Together, these results indicate a heavy-tailed distribution where the majority of claims are single-hop, with a minority that genuinely require multi-hop evidence integration. <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">On FEVER, tuning maximum retrieval hops shows performance peaking at 2 hops, consistent with the hypothesis that many claims can be resolved with one or two sentences, while deeper retrieval introduces noise</cite>.

- SciFact (Orig and Open) — open-domain science:
  <cite id="55e77ff1-1">SciFact-Open was constructed to mirror deployment realities by sampling 500K abstracts from S2ORC and including all evidence from SciFact-Orig, explicitly designed to assess verification over large, diverse scientific corpora</cite>. <cite id="55e77ff1-3">Evidence is distributed unequally: half of all evidence-carrying claim-article pairs (ECAPs) are allocated to 34 highly-studied claims (12% of all claims), and these tend to be short and mention common, well-studied entities, which retrieve four times as many documents in PubMed</cite>. This pattern suggests a long-tailed distribution of step requirements: a small set of canonical claims have abundant, quickly retrievable evidence and often need few steps, while many other claims require deeper search and integration due to sparse coverage or complex entities. <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Methodologically, SciFact is often converted from multi-evidence to binary claim-level labels and then sampled for evaluation, and LLM-based frameworks select world-knowledge-heavy subsets to approximate fact-checking difficulty</cite>.

- HOVER (Wikipedia multi-hop) — controlled multi-hop evaluation:
  <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER is explicitly partitioned into 2-, 3-, and 4-hop subsets, enabling hop-aware evaluation of multi-hop reasoning</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">In paired designs, HOVER-2/3/4 contain thousands of claims per hop level, and EX-FEVER primarily covers 2–3 hop chains over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-3">HOVER-2 (1,126 claims), HOVER-3 (1,835), and HOVER-4 (1,039) show a nontrivial, though minority, number of higher-hop instances</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-2">Recent LLM-augmented systems benchmark both FEVER (single-hop) and these HOVER subsets to probe single- and multi-hop performance jointly</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">Empirically, balanced stratified sampling across hop settings is used to ensure a representative distribution of multi-hop complexity at evaluation time</cite>.

- FEVEROUS (complex, mixed modalities):
  <cite id="7f1e03a9-0">FEVEROUS includes challenges such as multi-hop reasoning alongside numerical and entity-disambiguation tasks</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-1">Compared to HOVER, FEVEROUS presents additional challenges (distractors, longer passages) and is often treated as a single heterogeneous set including single-hop cases</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">Researchers commonly select FEVEROUS validation sets to probe numerical and multi-hop reasoning without full-scale data collection</cite>. Although hop-level breakdowns are less standardized than HOVER, FEVEROUS’s design implies a mixture where single-hop and shallow multi-hop claims are common, with a minority requiring deeper integration.

- LLM-era verification (chain-of-thought and hop-adaptive retrieval):
  <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Recent frameworks evaluate on SciFact and HOVER, framing verification as predicting True/False from paired evidence and explicitly sampling only 4-hop HOVER claims to test deep reasoning</cite>. This practice underscores that, even in modern benchmarks, the claims that require multi-step reasoning form a challenging tail, motivating targeted sampling and hop-adaptive retrieval strategies. <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">Across datasets, allowing up to two hops often yields near-optimal performance on FEVER-like data, while HOVER requires matching the claim’s hop depth (2, 3, or 4) to achieve peak accuracy, reflecting a distribution where reasoning depth correlates tightly with claim complexity</cite>.

Quantitative signals about step counts

- Shallow vs. deep reasoning: <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">On FEVER, accuracy peaks at 2 hops, indicating that most claims can be resolved with 1–2 evidence sentences; beyond two hops, added retrieval introduces redundant or irrelevant content that degrades accuracy</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">By contrast, HOVER subsets show optimal performance when retrieval is tuned to match hop length—2 hops for HOVER-2, 3 for HOVER-3, and 4 for HOVER-4—demonstrating that deeper chains are necessary for those claims and that models degrade when under- or over-hopping</cite>. Together, these results map a distribution where single-hop and 2-hop claims are the mode, and 3–4 hop claims form a minority but higher-variance tail.

- Evidence burden and skew: <cite id="55e77ff1-3">In SciFact-Open, 34 highly studied claims account for half of all evidence, with these claims being short and involving common entities that retrieve four times more documents on PubMed</cite>. This concentration implies that many claims require few steps due to abundant, authoritative sources, while the remaining majority face sparser, fragmented evidence that demands more iterative retrieval and integration steps to reach a verdict.

- Dataset design and multi-hop prevalence: <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER’s explicit hop partitioning (2–4) makes multi-hop the primary unit of evaluation, with each hop class containing thousands of claims</cite>, whereas <cite id="b52c4464-0">FEVER and related single-hop datasets are dominated by claims that can be decided from one or a few sentences, leading to shortcut biases if models overfit to single-path evidence</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER narrows hop depth primarily to 2–3, again suggesting a minority of deeper chains</cite>. When combined, these designs indicate a heavy-tailed distribution across scientific verification: a large core of single-hop claims with a long tail of multi-hop instances whose depth is dataset- and domain-specific.

Implications and modeling considerations

- Step budget and retrieval cost: <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">Because performance peaks near two hops on simpler datasets, cost-sensitive systems can often cap at two hops without significant accuracy loss while guarding against under-hopping</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-3">For complex claims, iterative, dependency-aware retrieval and reasoning (multi-hop) are necessary to link entities, events, and causal relations, and naive concatenation of claims with evidence can miss critical links</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">Balanced hop-stratified evaluation and training (e.g., equal ratios across 2–4 hops) help models generalize across step depths</cite>.

- Data bias and distribution shift: <cite id="b52c4464-0">Single-path biases are common; models can learn shortcut correlations that make multi-hop claims appear solvable with shallow evidence</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-4">Debiasing methods that account for multi-hop reasoning paths (e.g., causal walk) improve robustness and expose performance drops when spurious patterns are removed, highlighting that training distributions skewed toward shallow steps can mislead models</cite>.

- Domain and claim features shaping step counts: <cite id="55e77ff1-3">Short, entity-rich claims tied to well-studied topics concentrate most evidence and likely need fewer steps</cite>, whereas long-tail, niche, or multi-entity claims require deeper, iterative search and integration. <cite id="b52c4464-3">Causal/relational complexity further increases step requirements, motivating structured, stepwise retrieval rather than single-sentence similarity</cite>.

Limitations and open gaps

- Granular distributions: While HOVER provides clear hop-level breakdowns and FEVER-like data show optima around two hops, comprehensive hop histograms for datasets like PubHealth and SciQ are not standardized in current evaluations. <cite id="55e77ff1-0">PubHealth verifies public health claims against news/web sources; SciQ offers world-knowledge QA from literature</cite>, but hop-level annotations and step-length distributions remain underreported compared to HOVER/FEVEROUS. <cite id="7f1e03a9-1">Self-instruction and explainability models have reported FEVEROUS/HOER statistics but not full hop histograms</cite>. Publishing claim-level proof trees and step counts (number of retrieved snippets/facts and chain-of-thought depth) would enable precise histograms across datasets.

- LLM chain-of-thought depth: Modern verification systems frequently sample only 4-hop claims or filter for world-knowledge difficulty, which obscures the full step-length distribution at scale. <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Frameworks on SciFact and HOVER often restrict to challenging subsets to manage cost while probing deep reasoning</cite>.

Practical takeaway

- In practice, plan for a long-tailed distribution of reasoning steps: design for rapid resolution of 1–2 hop claims as the mode, while reserving iterative, structured multi-hop modules for the minority of complex claims. <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">Empirical optima suggest two hops as a reasonable default on many datasets</cite>, and <cite id="b52c4464-2">3–4 hop mechanisms are necessary on HOVER’s higher-hop subsets</cite>. <cite id="55e77ff1-3">Entity popularity and claim succinctness skew evidence availability and step counts</cite>. Finally, <cite id="b52c4464-0">debias training and evaluation to prevent shortcut learning that rewards shallow chains at the expense of true multi-hop reasoning</cite>.

However, in many cases, the process of verifying a claim requires integrating and reasoning over several pieces of evidence (Ostrowski et al. 2021). Therefore, multi-hop fact verification, which performs a multi-hop reasoning process to verify a claim, has become an attractive research topic recently (Zhou et al. 2019;Zhao et al. 2020a;Si, Zhu, and Zhou 2023). 

Though notable progress has been made, most multi-hop fact verification methods focus on learning label-specific features for judging the veracity of the given claim, which may expose the models to hidden data bias. Previous study (Schuster et al. 2019) has shown that there are annotation biases in a commonly used fact verification dataset, FEVER (Thorne et al. 2018), where most of the claims require only a single piece of evidence to verify. As shown in Figure 1, we observe that there are also biases in the multi-hop fact verification datasets such as PolitiHop (Ostrowski et al. 2021). The sentence "The post was flagged as part ..." appears 85 times in the training set of PolitiHop with a high correlation with the REFUTES label. Therefore, it is easy for the black-box neural network methods to learn such shortcut paths instead of multi-hop reasoning to cheat and obtain the right answer. We found obvious performance declines for some popular multi-hop fact verification methods when such biases are removed in a synthetic dataset. The same phenomenon, known as disconnected reasoning, has also been found in multi-hop question answering datasets (Trivedi et al. 2020). Previous methods for debiasing cannot deal with biases in multi-hop datasets as they mainly formulate fact verification as a single-hop reasoning task. For data augmentation-based methods (Wei and Zou 2019;Lee et al. 2021), it is difficult to generate unbiased multi-hop fact verification instances.

FEVEROUS (Aly et al., 2021) is a benchmark dataset for complex claim verification over structured and unstructured data. Each claim is annotated with evidence from sentences and forms in Wikipedia. SciFact-Open (Wadden et al., 2022a) is a testing dataset for scientific claim verification. This dataset aims to test existing models' claim verification performance in an open-domain setting. Since the claims in SciFact-Open do not have a global label, we select claims with complete evidence that either support or refute the claim and utilize them as the global label. Snippet: In the digital age, the unregulated spread of misinformation poses a profound threat to public understanding and societal stability. Automated fact verification has emerged as a critical tool to address this issue by evaluating whether a natural language claim aligns with established facts [1]. This task generally involves two core stages: retrieving relevant evidence from a large-scale knowledge corpus, and performing logical reasoning over the retrieved evidence to assess the claim's veracity [32]. Effective fact verification not only enhances the reliability of online content but also plays a vital role in safeguarding public discourse and democratic processes. 

Conventional fact verification methods typically rely on the semantic similarity between a claim and candidate evidence sentences to retrieve a relevant evidence set, which is then used to assess the claim's veracity [4], [6]. While this approach performs well for simple, straightforward claims, it often fails when handling complex claims, which require reasoning over Fig. 1. A complex claim requiring multi-hop reasoning over entities, events, and relational dependencies. multiple entities, events, relational dependencies, or causal relationships [10]. As illustrated in Figure 1, verifying whether a scientist received a Nobel Prize for a discovery that later contributed to technological advancement involves complex reasoning. This includes connecting multiple entities, events, and causal relations-such as award attribution, scientific contribution, and downstream impact. Traditional single-hop verification models lack mechanisms for linking information across evidence, often resulting in fragmented reasoning chains or missed critical evidence that render them ineffective for complex claims [7]. In contrast, multi-hop verification iteratively retrieves and integrates semantically linked evidence, offering a more robust framework for constructing coherent evidence sets and validating complex claims [15]. 

Multi-hop fact verification typically follows a stepwise retrieval process, where each query is generated from the claim and prior evidence to iteratively retrieve the next relevant piece, forming a complete set of evidence [25], [35]. By modeling inter-evidence dependencies during retrieval, these methods have demonstrated improved capacity for handling complex claims. Despite this progress, current multi-hop approaches face fundamental limitations. Firstly, in the retrieval stage, most systems generate the next-hop query by simply concatenating the claim with earlier evidence, without explicitly modeling the retrieving history [28].

Title: Causal Walk: Debiasing Multi-Hop Fact Verification with Front-Door Adjustment
Snippet: Multi-hop fact verification aims to detect the veracity of the given claim by integrating and reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence. Conventional multi-hop fact verification models are prone to rely on spurious correlations from the annotation artifacts, leading to an obvious performance decline on unbiased datasets. Among the various debiasing works, the causal inference-based methods become popular by performing theoretically guaranteed debiasing such as casual intervention or counterfactual reasoning. However, existing causal inference-based debiasing methods, which mainly formulate fact verification as a single-hop reasoning task to tackle shallow bias patterns, cannot deal with the complicated bias patterns hidden in multiple hops of evidence. To address the challenge, we propose Causal Walk, a novel method for debiasing multi-hop fact verification from a causal perspective with front-door adjustment. Specifically, in the structural causal model, the reasoning path between the treatment (the input claim-evidence graph) and the outcome (the veracity label) is introduced as the mediator to block the confounder. With the front-door adjustment, the causal effect between the treatment and the outcome is decomposed into the causal effect between the treatment and the mediator, which is estimated by applying the idea of random walk, and the causal effect between the mediator and the outcome, which is estimated with normalized weighted geometric mean approximation. To investigate the effectiveness of the proposed method, an adversarial multi-hop fact verification dataset and a symmetric multi-hop fact verification dataset are proposed with the help of the large language model. Experimental results show that Causal Walk outperforms some previous debiasing methods on both existing datasets and the newly constructed datasets. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/zcccccz/CausalWalk.
