Snippet: In this section, we describe the construction of SCIFACT-OPEN. We report the performance of claim verification models on SCIFACT-OPEN in §4, and perform reliability checks on the results in §5. 

Our goal is to construct a test collection which can be used to assess the performance of claim verification systems deployed on a large corpus of scientific literature. This requires a collection of claims, a corpus of abstracts against which to verify them, and evidence annotations with which to evaluate system predictions. We use the claims from the SCIFACT-ORIG test set as our claims for SCIFACT-OPEN.2 To obtain evidence annotations, we use all evidence from SCIFACT-ORIG as evidence in our new dataset and collect additional evidence from the SCIFACT-OPEN corpus. 

For our corpus, we filter the S2ORC dataset (Lo et al., 2020) for all articles which (1) cover topics related to medicine or biology and (2) have at least one inbound and one outbound citation. From the roughly 6.5 million articles that pass these filters, we randomly sample 500K articles to form the corpus for SCIFACT-OPEN, making sure to include the 5K abstracts from SCIFACT-ORIG. We choose to limit the corpus to 500K abstracts to ensure that we can achieve sufficient annotation coverage of the available evidence. Additional details on corpus construction can be found in Appendix A. 

Unlike SCIFACT-ORIG (which is skewed toward highly-cited articles from "high-impact" journals), we do not impose any additional quality filters on articles included in SCIFACT-OPEN; thus, our corpus captures the full diversity of information likely to be encountered when scientific fact-checking systems are deployed on real-world resources like S2ORC, arXiv, 3 or PubMed Central. 4

Title: Reasoning Paths as Signals: Augmenting Multi-Hop Fact Verification Through Structural Reasoning Progression
Snippet: To examine how the number of retrieved evidence hops affects overall verification performance, we conduct the hyperparameter analysis on the FEVER dataset and the three subsets of HoVer. Summary

Across scientific fact-verification datasets, the number of reasoning steps needed to verify a claim typically falls into two regimes: a large majority of claims can be resolved with one or two evidence pieces (single- or shallow multi-hop), while a minority require deeper multi-hop chains (often 3–4 hops) that integrate multiple documents and relations; the proportion and depth of multi-hop reasoning vary systematically with dataset design and domain coverage. <cite id="b52c4464-0">In many public datasets, most claims require only a single piece of evidence, and multi-hop datasets can also contain shortcut biases that make single-path verification easy if not carefully controlled</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER explicitly stratifies claims into 2-, 3-, and 4-hop reasoning, reflecting a minority of deep multi-hop instances</cite>, and <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER likewise emphasizes primarily 2–3 hop reasoning over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>. Empirical analyses show that models often achieve peak accuracy at around two hops on simpler data like FEVER, indicating that many claims are verifiable with shallow chains, while multi-hop datasets require tuning to match the claim’s reasoning depth. <cite id="55e77ff1-3">SciFact-Open further shows an unequal allocation of evidence across claims, with a small fraction of well-studied, short, entity-rich claims consuming most evidence and likely requiring fewer steps</cite>.

What constitutes a “reasoning step”

In scientific claim verification, a “reasoning step” can be measured in several equivalent ways: number of evidence hops retrieved (query iterations linking entities and events across documents), number of integrated facts used to derive a logical conclusion, or depth of chain-of-thought linking premises to the claim. <cite id="b52c4464-3">Complex claims require iterative retrieval and logical integration over multiple entities, events, and causal relations, often implemented as stepwise retrieval where each query is generated from the claim and prior evidence to form a complete evidence set</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER formalizes this by grouping claims by the number of hops across passages</cite>, and <cite id="55e77ff1-4">HoVER is widely used to evaluate 4-hop reasoning</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER focuses on 2–3 hop chains over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>.

Distributions by dataset

- FEVER and FEVER-like sources (PubMed/Wikipedia): single-hop dominance with occasional multi-hop.
  <cite id="b52c4464-0">Prior work on FEVER found that most claims require only a single piece of evidence to verify, and models can exploit annotation artifacts or shortcut paths</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-4">Debiasing methods revealed that even multi-hop datasets can hide spurious correlations, and performance can drop when such shortcuts are removed</cite>. Together, these results indicate a heavy-tailed distribution where the majority of claims are single-hop, with a minority that genuinely require multi-hop evidence integration. <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">On FEVER, tuning maximum retrieval hops shows performance peaking at 2 hops, consistent with the hypothesis that many claims can be resolved with one or two sentences, while deeper retrieval introduces noise</cite>.

- SciFact (Orig and Open) — open-domain science:
  <cite id="55e77ff1-1">SciFact-Open was constructed to mirror deployment realities by sampling 500K abstracts from S2ORC and including all evidence from SciFact-Orig, explicitly designed to assess verification over large, diverse scientific corpora</cite>. <cite id="55e77ff1-3">Evidence is distributed unequally: half of all evidence-carrying claim-article pairs (ECAPs) are allocated to 34 highly-studied claims (12% of all claims), and these tend to be short and mention common, well-studied entities, which retrieve four times as many documents in PubMed</cite>. This pattern suggests a long-tailed distribution of step requirements: a small set of canonical claims have abundant, quickly retrievable evidence and often need few steps, while many other claims require deeper search and integration due to sparse coverage or complex entities. <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Methodologically, SciFact is often converted from multi-evidence to binary claim-level labels and then sampled for evaluation, and LLM-based frameworks select world-knowledge-heavy subsets to approximate fact-checking difficulty</cite>.

- HOVER (Wikipedia multi-hop) — controlled multi-hop evaluation:
  <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER is explicitly partitioned into 2-, 3-, and 4-hop subsets, enabling hop-aware evaluation of multi-hop reasoning</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">In paired designs, HOVER-2/3/4 contain thousands of claims per hop level, and EX-FEVER primarily covers 2–3 hop chains over hyperlinked Wikipedia</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-3">HOVER-2 (1,126 claims), HOVER-3 (1,835), and HOVER-4 (1,039) show a nontrivial, though minority, number of higher-hop instances</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-2">Recent LLM-augmented systems benchmark both FEVER (single-hop) and these HOVER subsets to probe single- and multi-hop performance jointly</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">Empirically, balanced stratified sampling across hop settings is used to ensure a representative distribution of multi-hop complexity at evaluation time</cite>.

- FEVEROUS (complex, mixed modalities):
  <cite id="7f1e03a9-0">FEVEROUS includes challenges such as multi-hop reasoning alongside numerical and entity-disambiguation tasks</cite>. <cite id="7f1e03a9-1">Compared to HOVER, FEVEROUS presents additional challenges (distractors, longer passages) and is often treated as a single heterogeneous set including single-hop cases</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-1">Researchers commonly select FEVEROUS validation sets to probe numerical and multi-hop reasoning without full-scale data collection</cite>. Although hop-level breakdowns are less standardized than HOVER, FEVEROUS’s design implies a mixture where single-hop and shallow multi-hop claims are common, with a minority requiring deeper integration.

- LLM-era verification (chain-of-thought and hop-adaptive retrieval):
  <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Recent frameworks evaluate on SciFact and HOVER, framing verification as predicting True/False from paired evidence and explicitly sampling only 4-hop HOVER claims to test deep reasoning</cite>. This practice underscores that, even in modern benchmarks, the claims that require multi-step reasoning form a challenging tail, motivating targeted sampling and hop-adaptive retrieval strategies. <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">Across datasets, allowing up to two hops often yields near-optimal performance on FEVER-like data, while HOVER requires matching the claim’s hop depth (2, 3, or 4) to achieve peak accuracy, reflecting a distribution where reasoning depth correlates tightly with claim complexity</cite>.

Quantitative signals about step counts

- Shallow vs. deep reasoning: <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">On FEVER, accuracy peaks at 2 hops, indicating that most claims can be resolved with 1–2 evidence sentences; beyond two hops, added retrieval introduces redundant or irrelevant content that degrades accuracy</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">By contrast, HOVER subsets show optimal performance when retrieval is tuned to match hop length—2 hops for HOVER-2, 3 for HOVER-3, and 4 for HOVER-4—demonstrating that deeper chains are necessary for those claims and that models degrade when under- or over-hopping</cite>. Together, these results map a distribution where single-hop and 2-hop claims are the mode, and 3–4 hop claims form a minority but higher-variance tail.

- Evidence burden and skew: <cite id="55e77ff1-3">In SciFact-Open, 34 highly studied claims account for half of all evidence, with these claims being short and involving common entities that retrieve four times more documents on PubMed</cite>. This concentration implies that many claims require few steps due to abundant, authoritative sources, while the remaining majority face sparser, fragmented evidence that demands more iterative retrieval and integration steps to reach a verdict.

- Dataset design and multi-hop prevalence: <cite id="b52c4464-1">HOVER’s explicit hop partitioning (2–4) makes multi-hop the primary unit of evaluation, with each hop class containing thousands of claims</cite>, whereas <cite id="b52c4464-0">FEVER and related single-hop datasets are dominated by claims that can be decided from one or a few sentences, leading to shortcut biases if models overfit to single-path evidence</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">EX-FEVER narrows hop depth primarily to 2–3, again suggesting a minority of deeper chains</cite>. When combined, these designs indicate a heavy-tailed distribution across scientific verification: a large core of single-hop claims with a long tail of multi-hop instances whose depth is dataset- and domain-specific.

Implications and modeling considerations

- Step budget and retrieval cost: <cite id="7f1e03a9-4">Because performance peaks near two hops on simpler datasets, cost-sensitive systems can often cap at two hops without significant accuracy loss while guarding against under-hopping</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-3">For complex claims, iterative, dependency-aware retrieval and reasoning (multi-hop) are necessary to link entities, events, and causal relations, and naive concatenation of claims with evidence can miss critical links</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-2">Balanced hop-stratified evaluation and training (e.g., equal ratios across 2–4 hops) help models generalize across step depths</cite>.

- Data bias and distribution shift: <cite id="b52c4464-0">Single-path biases are common; models can learn shortcut correlations that make multi-hop claims appear solvable with shallow evidence</cite>. <cite id="b52c4464-4">Debiasing methods that account for multi-hop reasoning paths (e.g., causal walk) improve robustness and expose performance drops when spurious patterns are removed, highlighting that training distributions skewed toward shallow steps can mislead models</cite>.

- Domain and claim features shaping step counts: <cite id="55e77ff1-3">Short, entity-rich claims tied to well-studied topics concentrate most evidence and likely need fewer steps</cite>, whereas long-tail, niche, or multi-entity claims require deeper, iterative search and integration. <cite id="b52c4464-3">Causal/relational complexity further increases step requirements, motivating structured, stepwise retrieval rather than single-sentence similarity</cite>.

Limitations and open gaps

- Granular distributions: While HOVER provides clear hop-level breakdowns and FEVER-like data show optima around two hops, comprehensive hop histograms for datasets like PubHealth and SciQ are not standardized in current evaluations. <cite id="55e77ff1-0">PubHealth verifies public health claims against news/web sources; SciQ offers world-knowledge QA from literature</cite>, but hop-level annotations and step-length distributions remain underreported compared to HOVER/FEVEROUS. <cite id="7f1e03a9-1">Self-instruction and explainability models have reported FEVEROUS/HOER statistics but not full hop histograms</cite>. Publishing claim-level proof trees and step counts (number of retrieved snippets/facts and chain-of-thought depth) would enable precise histograms across datasets.

- LLM chain-of-thought depth: Modern verification systems frequently sample only 4-hop claims or filter for world-knowledge difficulty, which obscures the full step-length distribution at scale. <cite id="55e77ff1-4">Frameworks on SciFact and HOVER often restrict to challenging subsets to manage cost while probing deep reasoning</cite>.

Practical takeaway

Finally, <cite id="b52c4464-0">debias training and evaluation to prevent shortcut learning that rewards shallow chains at the expense of true multi-hop reasoning</cite>.

Title: Reasoning Paths as Signals: Augmenting Multi-Hop Fact Verification Through Structural Reasoning Progression
Snippet: In the digital age, the unregulated spread of misinformation poses a profound threat to public understanding and societal stability. Automated fact verification has emerged as a critical tool to address this issue by evaluating whether a natural language claim aligns with established facts [1]. This task generally involves two core stages: retrieving relevant evidence from a large-scale knowledge corpus, and performing logical reasoning over the retrieved evidence to assess the claim's veracity [32]. Effective fact verification not only enhances the reliability of online content but also plays a vital role in safeguarding public discourse and democratic processes. 

Conventional fact verification methods typically rely on the semantic similarity between a claim and candidate evidence sentences to retrieve a relevant evidence set, which is then used to assess the claim's veracity [4], [6]. While this approach performs well for simple, straightforward claims, it often fails when handling complex claims, which require reasoning over Fig. 1. A complex claim requiring multi-hop reasoning over entities, events, and relational dependencies. multiple entities, events, relational dependencies, or causal relationships [10]. As illustrated in Figure 1, verifying whether a scientist received a Nobel Prize for a discovery that later contributed to technological advancement involves complex reasoning. This includes connecting multiple entities, events, and causal relations-such as award attribution, scientific contribution, and downstream impact. Traditional single-hop verification models lack mechanisms for linking information across evidence, often resulting in fragmented reasoning chains or missed critical evidence that render them ineffective for complex claims [7]. In contrast, multi-hop verification iteratively retrieves and integrates semantically linked evidence, offering a more robust framework for constructing coherent evidence sets and validating complex claims [15]. 

Multi-hop fact verification typically follows a stepwise retrieval process, where each query is generated from the claim and prior evidence to iteratively retrieve the next relevant piece, forming a complete set of evidence [25], [35]. By modeling inter-evidence dependencies during retrieval, these methods have demonstrated improved capacity for handling complex claims. Despite this progress, current multi-hop approaches face fundamental limitations. Firstly, in the retrieval stage, most systems generate the next-hop query by simply concatenating the claim with earlier evidence, without explicitly modeling the retrieving history [28].

Title: Causal Walk: Debiasing Multi-Hop Fact Verification with Front-Door Adjustment
Snippet: Multi-hop fact verification aims to detect the veracity of the given claim by integrating and reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence. Conventional multi-hop fact verification models are prone to rely on spurious correlations from the annotation artifacts, leading to an obvious performance decline on unbiased datasets. Among the various debiasing works, the causal inference-based methods become popular by performing theoretically guaranteed debiasing such as casual intervention or counterfactual reasoning. However, existing causal inference-based debiasing methods, which mainly formulate fact verification as a single-hop reasoning task to tackle shallow bias patterns, cannot deal with the complicated bias patterns hidden in multiple hops of evidence. To address the challenge, we propose Causal Walk, a novel method for debiasing multi-hop fact verification from a causal perspective with front-door adjustment. Specifically, in the structural causal model, the reasoning path between the treatment (the input claim-evidence graph) and the outcome (the veracity label) is introduced as the mediator to block the confounder. With the front-door adjustment, the causal effect between the treatment and the outcome is decomposed into the causal effect between the treatment and the mediator, which is estimated by applying the idea of random walk, and the causal effect between the mediator and the outcome, which is estimated with normalized weighted geometric mean approximation. To investigate the effectiveness of the proposed method, an adversarial multi-hop fact verification dataset and a symmetric multi-hop fact verification dataset are proposed with the help of the large language model. Experimental results show that Causal Walk outperforms some previous debiasing methods on both existing datasets and the newly constructed datasets. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/zcccccz/CausalWalk.

Title: Two Contrasting Data Annotation Paradigms for Subjective NLP Tasks
Snippet: Several scientific claim verification datasets have been released in the past few years. COVIDFact (Saakyan et al., 2021) and HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) verify COVID-19 claims against scientific literature. PUBHEALTH (Kotonya and Toni, 2020) verifies public health claims against news and web sources. SCIFACT (Wadden et al., 2020) verifies claims made in citations in scientific papers. CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020) verifies claims about climate change against Wikipedia. In this work, our focus is verifying claims against scientific literature. We therefore perform experiments on the COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SCIFACT datasets. Preprocessing details and summary statistics for these datasets are included in §4.1.

Title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Snippet: In this section, we describe the construction of SCIFACT-OPEN. We report the performance of claim verification models on SCIFACT-OPEN in §4, and perform reliability checks on the results in §5. 

Our goal is to construct a test collection which can be used to assess the performance of claim verification systems deployed on a large corpus of scientific literature. This requires a collection of claims, a corpus of abstracts against which to verify them, and evidence annotations with which to evaluate system predictions. We use the claims from the SCIFACT-ORIG test set as our claims for SCIFACT-OPEN.2 To obtain evidence annotations, we use all evidence from SCIFACT-ORIG as evidence in our new dataset and collect additional evidence from the SCIFACT-OPEN corpus. 

For our corpus, we filter the S2ORC dataset (Lo et al., 2020) for all articles which (1) cover topics related to medicine or biology and (2) have at least one inbound and one outbound citation. From the roughly 6.5 million articles that pass these filters, we randomly sample 500K articles to form the corpus for SCIFACT-OPEN, making sure to include the 5K abstracts from SCIFACT-ORIG. We choose to limit the corpus to 500K abstracts to ensure that we can achieve sufficient annotation coverage of the available evidence. Additional details on corpus construction can be found in Appendix A. 

Unlike SCIFACT-ORIG (which is skewed toward highly-cited articles from "high-impact" journals), we do not impose any additional quality filters on articles included in SCIFACT-OPEN; thus, our corpus captures the full diversity of information likely to be encountered when scientific fact-checking systems are deployed on real-world resources like S2ORC, arXiv, 3 or PubMed Central. 4

Title: MedS³: Towards Medical Slow Thinking with Self-Evolved Soft Dual-sided Process Supervision
Snippet: Please also provide a brief explanation of your score. 

Give your score in the following format: <score>{{Your score}}</score> Question: {question} Response: {response} in the dataset spans multiple medical specialties, making it an ideal resource for creating models capable of assisting healthcare professionals in making informed diagnostic decisions. Due to its huge test set (over 100,000 test instances), we randomly select 2,000 items for evaluation. 8. SciQ (Welbl, Liu, and Gardner 2017) is a scientific question-answering dataset designed to assess machine learning models in answering factual questions across a wide range of scientific domains. It consists of over 13,000 questions derived from scientific literature, including topics in physics, biology, chemistry, and earth sciences, among others. Each question is paired with a correct answer and is supported by a passage of text from which the answer is extracted. 9. Evidence Inference (DeYoung et al. 2020) is a collection designed to evaluate machine learning models on their ability to infer logical conclusions from evidence presented in the form of textual information. This dataset consists of structured pairs of premises (evidence) and hypotheses, where the goal is for models to determine the logical relationship between them-whether the hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or is neutral with respect to the provided evidence. Typically used for tasks such as textual entailment or natural language inference (NLI), the dataset includes a variety of complex scenarios across multiple domains, including law, healthcare, and science, where reasoning based on available evidence is crucial. 10. PubHealth (Kotonya and Toni 2020) is a comprehensive dataset for explainable automated fact-checking of public health claims. Each instance in the PUBHEALTH dataset has an associated veracity label (true, false, unproven, mixture). Furthermore, each instance in the dataset has an explanation text field. The explanation is a justification for which the claim has been assigned a particular veracity label. We construct two different test sets. Healthfact is to directly predict whether a given instance is true/false/unproven/mixture. The other, Pubhealth, is to predict whether the instance sentence and the given explanation express the same meaning. 11.

Title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Snippet: We observe three properties of evidence in SCIFACT-OPEN that have received less attention in the study of scientific claim verification, and that can inform future work on this task. 

Unequal allocation of evidence Fig. 3 shows the distribution of evidence amongst claims in SCIFACT-OPEN. We find that evidence is distributed unequally; half of all ECAPs are allocated to 34 highly-studied claims (12% of all claims in the dataset). We investigated the characteristics of highly-studied claims, and found that they tend to 0 1 2 3 4 5   be short and mention a small number of common, well-studied scientific entities. For instance, entities mentioned in well-studied claims (≥ 4 ECAPs) return, on average, 4 times as many documents when entered into a PubMed search, compared to claims with no evidence (detailed results in Appendix B). Table 3 shows an example.

Title: Fact-Checking with Large Language Models via Probabilistic Certainty and Consistency
Snippet: We evaluate our framework on three challenging fact-checking datasets: SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020), FeLMWk (Zhao et al., 2023), and HoVER (Jiang et al., 2020). Each dataset consists of natural language claims paired with ground-truth factual labels (True or False). Below we summarize the key characteristics and preprocessing choices for each dataset: 

• SciFact: This dataset contains expert-written scientific claims derived from PubMed abstracts, each paired with annotated evidence. The original evidence-level labels include Support, Refute, and Not Enough Info. To ensure consistency, we convert this to a binary claimlevel format by (i) filtering out claims with contradictory labels across evidence and (ii) excluding claims associated with Not Enough Info. Following prior work (Xie et al., 2025) and to control API costs, we sample 187 claims for our experiments. 

• FeLMWk: This dataset consists of claims generated by LLMs across diverse domains, annotated with fine-grained factuality labels. For our evaluation, we select the subset of claims that require world knowledge for verification, which is the closest setting to fact-checking. 

• HoVER: This dataset contains multi-hop claims that require reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence. Each claim is associated with a Wikipedia passage set, and the difficulty increases with hop length. We focus on the most challenging 4-hop claims, which demand reasoning over several interconnected evidence spans. To reduce API costs while preserving difficulty, we sample 190 claims for evaluation.

snippet.text: Several scientific claim verification datasets have been released in the past few years. COVIDFact (Saakyan et al., 2021) and HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) verify COVID-19 claims against scientific literature. PUBHEALTH (Kotonya and Toni, 2020) verifies public health claims against news and web sources. SCIFACT (Wadden et al., 2020) verifies claims made in citations in scientific papers. CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020) verifies claims about climate change against Wikipedia. In this work, our focus is verifying claims against scientific literature. We therefore perform experiments on the COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SCIFACT datasets. Preprocessing details and summary statistics for these datasets are included in §4.1.

In this section, we describe the construction of SCIFACT-OPEN. We report the performance of claim verification models on SCIFACT-OPEN in §4, and perform reliability checks on the results in §5. 

Our goal is to construct a test collection which can be used to assess the performance of claim verification systems deployed on a large corpus of scientific literature. This requires a collection of claims, a corpus of abstracts against which to verify them, and evidence annotations with which to evaluate system predictions. We use the claims from the SCIFACT-ORIG test set as our claims for SCIFACT-OPEN.2 To obtain evidence annotations, we use all evidence from SCIFACT-ORIG as evidence in our new dataset and collect additional evidence from the SCIFACT-OPEN corpus. 

For our corpus, we filter the S2ORC dataset (Lo et al., 2020) for all articles which (1) cover topics related to medicine or biology and (2) have at least one inbound and one outbound citation. From the roughly 6.5 million articles that pass these filters, we randomly sample 500K articles to form the corpus for SCIFACT-OPEN, making sure to include the 5K abstracts from SCIFACT-ORIG. We choose to limit the corpus to 500K abstracts to ensure that we can achieve sufficient annotation coverage of the available evidence. Additional details on corpus construction can be found in Appendix A. 

Unlike SCIFACT-ORIG (which is skewed toward highly-cited articles from "high-impact" journals), we do not impose any additional quality filters on articles included in SCIFACT-OPEN; thus, our corpus captures the full diversity of information likely to be encountered when scientific fact-checking systems are deployed on real-world resources like S2ORC, arXiv, 3 or PubMed Central. 4

Due to its huge test set (over 100,000 test instances), we randomly select 2,000 items for evaluation. 8. SciQ (Welbl, Liu, and Gardner 2017) is a scientific question-answering dataset designed to assess machine learning models in answering factual questions across a wide range of scientific domains. It consists of over 13,000 questions derived from scientific literature, including topics in physics, biology, chemistry, and earth sciences, among others. Each question is paired with a correct answer and is supported by a passage of text from which the answer is extracted. 9. Evidence Inference (DeYoung et al. 2020) is a collection designed to evaluate machine learning models on their ability to infer logical conclusions from evidence presented in the form of textual information. This dataset consists of structured pairs of premises (evidence) and hypotheses, where the goal is for models to determine the logical relationship between them-whether the hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or is neutral with respect to the provided evidence. Typically used for tasks such as textual entailment or natural language inference (NLI), the dataset includes a variety of complex scenarios across multiple domains, including law, healthcare, and science, where reasoning based on available evidence is crucial. 10. PubHealth (Kotonya and Toni 2020) is a comprehensive dataset for explainable automated fact-checking of public health claims. Each instance in the PUBHEALTH dataset has an associated veracity label (true, false, unproven, mixture). Furthermore, each instance in the dataset has an explanation text field. The explanation is a justification for which the claim has been assigned a particular veracity label. We construct two different test sets. Healthfact is to directly predict whether a given instance is true/false/unproven/mixture. The other, Pubhealth, is to predict whether the instance sentence and the given explanation express the same meaning. 11.

We observe three properties of evidence in SCIFACT-OPEN that have received less attention in the study of scientific claim verification, and that can inform future work on this task. 

Unequal allocation of evidence Fig. 3 shows the distribution of evidence amongst claims in SCIFACT-OPEN. We find that evidence is distributed unequally; half of all ECAPs are allocated to 34 highly-studied claims (12% of all claims in the dataset). We investigated the characteristics of highly-studied claims, and found that they tend to 0 1 2 3 4 5   be short and mention a small number of common, well-studied scientific entities. For instance, entities mentioned in well-studied claims (≥ 4 ECAPs) return, on average, 4 times as many documents when entered into a PubMed search, compared to claims with no evidence (detailed results in Appendix B). Title: Mining the Explainability and Generalization: Fact Verification Based on Self-Instruction
Snippet: We evaluate the performance of our model using two datasets, FEVEROUS and HOVER.

FEVEROUS is proposed by Aly et al. (2021), consisting of fact-checking data with various challenges such as Numerical Reasoning, Entity Disambiguation, and Multi-hop Reasoning.

HOVER was proposed by Yang et al. (2018), which serves as a more challenging multi-hop factchecking dataset, with a maximum hop count of 4. This is attributed not only to the increased number of hops but also to the longer evidence provided, most of which contain distracting information.Appendix C presents detailed statistical data for the two datasets.

Title: Coordinating Search-Informed Reasoning and Reasoning-Guided Search in Claim Verification
Snippet: A.1 Dataset HOVER (Jiang et al., 2020) is a multi-hop claim verification dataset containing 2, 3, and 4-hop data, designed to evaluate the ability of models to connect multiple pieces of evidence across different documents. EX-FEVER (Ma et al., 2024) is another multi-hop benchmark, primarily focused on 2 and 3-hop reasoning over hyperlinked Wikipedia documents. 

For training, we sample 7,200 examples from the combined training sets of EX-FEVER and HOVER, maintaining an equal ratio across different hop lengths to ensure balanced coverage of multi-hop reasoning. 

For evaluation, we follow Wang and Shu ( 2023) and use stratified sampling to select 500 instances for each hop setting, ensuring a balanced distribution of multi-hop complexity. 

We also evaluate on CHECKWHY (Si et al., 2024), a challenging claim verification dataset where negative samples are constructed by modifying evidence to create counterfactuals. Given this design, we only sample from the positive claims and use accuracy for evaluation.

Title: Enhancing Multi-Hop Fact Verification with Structured Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Models
Snippet: To evaluate the effectiveness of LLM-SKAN for both singlehop and multi-hop fact verification tasks, we choose 4 public benchmarks, FEVER (Thorne et al. 2018b) and 2-, 3-, and 4-hop HOVER (Jiang et al. 2020), to conduct experiments. FEVER collects more than 180,000 humangenerated claims with retrieved evidence from Wikipedia 2 for single-hop fact verification and they are categorized into Supported, Refuted, and NEI. HOVER contains more than 15,000 claims that need multi-hop thinking to verify and retrieves evidence from Wikipedia for multi-hop fact verification. Each claim is labelled Supported and Not-Supported. It contains three sub-datasets, 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop HOVER. The statistics are shown in Table 2.

Snippet: In line with existing research, we have selected two publicly available datasets to assess the performance of EACon.Evaluation is carried out using the validation set.The chosen datasets are HOVER (Jiang et al. 2020) and FEVEROUS-S (Aly et al. 2021).

• HOVER The HOVER dataset comprises claims that necessitate verification through multiple pieces of evidence and multi-hop reasoning.It is organized into three subsets, each corresponding to a different level of reasoning complexity based on the number of hops.Specifically, the two-hop subset (HOVER-2) consists of 1,126 claims, the three-hop subset (HOVER-3) comprises 1,835 claims, and the four-hop (HOVER-4) subset includes 1,039 claims.• FEVEROUS-S FEVEROUS is a fact-checking dataset designed to validate claims using both structured and unstructured data sources.Our experimentation is focused on a subset of FEVEROUS, known as FEVEROUS-S, which exclusively involves claims that rely on unstructured data.In terms of claim complexity, it is noted that the claims in the HOVER dataset exhibit higher complexity compared to those in FEVEROUS-S.

Given our emphasis on the claim verification task, all experiments are executed using the evidence provided within the dataset (referred to as golden evidence).The performance is assessed using the Macro-F1 score as the evaluation metric.

Title: Reasoning Paths as Signals: Augmenting Multi-Hop Fact Verification Through Structural Reasoning Progression
Snippet: To examine how the number of retrieved evidence hops affects overall verification performance, we conduct the hyperparameter analysis on the FEVER dataset and the three subsets of HoVer. By varying the maximum number of retrieval hops, we aim to understand the trade-off between information sufficiency and noise accumulation across claims of different complexity levels. As shown in Figure 3, the optimal number of retrieval hops varies by dataset. On FEVER, performance peaks at 2 hops, indicating that most claims can be verified with one or two sentences. In contrast, the optimal hop counts for the 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop subsets of HoVer are 2, 3, and 4, respectively-demonstrating that our model adapts well to the reasoning depth required by each claim category. 

These results confirm that retrieving too few evidence sentences may lead to insufficient factual grounding, while excessive retrieval introduces redundant or irrelevant information, increasing reasoning difficulty and degrading final verification accuracy. Properly tuning the number of hops is therefore critical for balancing completeness and conciseness in multi-hop fact verification.
